Segment 1 · About me

From the chair to the channel

I didn't start YouTube to become a YouTuber. I started because I was tired of correcting the same misinformation in my chair every week while somebody with massive reach and zero expertise taught it wrong to thousands.

Story beat Tell this one like a storytime, not a résumé. Pick one specific client moment where you corrected something they learned online. That moment is your "why." Pause after it and ask the question below.
2018

ClutchNLoc starts as a mobile loctician

Going to clients, building the book one install at a time. The work was my marketing: before and afters, word of mouth, and clients sending clients.

Before YT

Showing up on Instagram

I posted my work for visibility, trust, and proof. It built my book, but a 30-second clip couldn't hold everything I wanted to teach.

May 2, 2024

I pressed upload

I shifted my attention to YouTube because it fit how I edit and how I teach. I like to explain the why, show the process, and tell the story. Short-form kept cutting me off mid-thought. Long-form let me be the educator.

The shift

Authority, but not "just a loctician"

I wanted to be seen as the expert in my space without being boxed in as only a loctician. So I built a personal brand instead of a service menu: a universe where what I love and what I do for a living feed each other.

Why I really started

I built the channel I needed

I was thinking about my younger self, and what I needed when I was trying to figure out what to do with my life or how to do a certain technique. When I started, I struggled to find information, to find out how to even start, and to find mentorship.

So I hope someone comes across me and I can be the help and the source I didn't have.

I also wanted to leave something behind. Something of substance that can still feed and teach people, and that my child and my family can go back to and see the footprint I left on this world.

This channel is my legacy, rooted in ethics and morals, because I ain't about to put no BS out there.

For my younger self

The info and mentorship I couldn't find.

For my family

A footprint my child can go back to.

For whoever finds me

A source that keeps teaching, even when I'm not in the room.

Bringing other interests into a "loctician channel" was intentional. I'm more than a loctician, and I know other people share the things I love outside the chair.

Who are you making this for? Picture one person: a younger you, a future client, your kids.

The universe I started with

Three pillars that all point back to me. Each one brings in a different viewer, and every viewer meets the brand. They have evolved since. You will see where they are now in a minute.

Locs

The craft. Installs, maintenance, corrections, education. This is the authority pillar and where search traffic comes from.

Business

How I run it: pricing, booking, systems, building offers. This is where other pros find me and where classes and products sell.

Lifestyle

Day in the life, the salon, the studio, who I am outside the service. This is what turns viewers into people who feel like they know me.

When someone finds you online, what do you want them to think you are? Just a service, or a person they'd follow even if they never book?
Segment 2 · The purpose of all this

Put the pros back in front

Right now your clients are learning from people who are only the expert of their own head. A DIYer can tell you what worked for them. We can tell you what works, why it works, and what to do when it doesn't, because we've seen it on hundreds of heads.

The DIY voice

Expert of one head

  • Teaches what worked for them, once
  • Has the reach and shows up consistently
  • Audience copies it, and some of them end up in our chairs needing a correction
The pro

Expert of the craft

  • Sees every texture, density, and mistake
  • Knows the why and the fix
  • Too often invisible online, so the audience never hears from us

What the DIY side is posting

These creators are documenting their own hair journeys, and audiences are learning from them. That's real content for their journey. It's also where your future clients are getting their information.

Indybindy · 362K subscribers"My First DIY Microloc Retie" next to beauty maintenance vlogs
Life of a Dreamer · 10.9K subscribersDIY microloc journey, loc sprinkles, human hair extensions
Naturally Ginger"I tried microlocs with extensions," 1-year and 11-month updates
The audience can't tell the difference until we show up.
Say it plainly This isn't about bashing DIYers. Their content is real for their journey. Our job is to balance it with expertise, so people hear from someone who does this every day.

Key things I learned

The service isn't the video

A two-hour retwist is not content. The story around it is. Channels in our industry die when they only film the service.

Fewer, better videos

I didn't chase daily trends. 18 strong long-form videos did more than 100 rushed ones would have.

Search is a slow burn that pays forever

The videos answering real client questions keep pulling views years later. Your chair questions are your best titles.

Systems beat motivation

Hands-free mounts and batch filming meant content never added time to an appointment.

Your audience tells you who they are

Analytics told me they watch on TV. I built for that and watch time went up.

YouTube is a business tool first

AdSense is the cherry. The bookings, classes, and partnerships it brings in are the cake.

Segment 4 · Leverage

One channel, many income streams

Ad revenue is one stream. The bigger win is that every video works as a sales rep for your chair, your classes, your products, and brands that want to reach your audience.

Stream 1

Booking

Booking link in every description, pinned comment, and channel link. Viewers arrive already trusting you, so consults convert.

Stream 2

Classes & coaching

Teach what you do. My microloc class, consultations, and coaching calls sell because people have watched me teach for free first.

Stream 3

Digital products

Guides and workbooks that answer the questions you get every week. Make it once, sell it under every related video.

Stream 4

Brand partnerships

Brands pay for trusted educators, not just big follower counts. BetterHelp sponsored one of my Locumentary episodes.

BetterHelp · 4 Years of Loc Growth ↗
Stream 5

Affiliate & storefront

Link the tools and products you already use. Your Amazon storefront and tool affiliates earn while you sleep.

Stream 6

AdSense

Real money once you qualify, and it grows with your library. Treat it as a bonus, not the plan.

How a single video pays you

Viewer finds "Why your starter locs are unraveling" in search → watches you fix it → clicks your booking link or buys your aftercare guide → subscribes → sees your next class announcement → becomes a client, a student, or a fan who shares you.

Which of these streams do you already have, even a little? Which one could you add in the next 90 days?
Segment 5 · Before we build anything
Don't let the niche talk stop you from starting.

If you spend weeks deciding your pillars, your look, and exactly how to present yourself, you'll delay starting or never start. At the end of the day, we know what your channel is: it's you and your profession.

Focus on this

You plus your trade. That's the whole starting point. I already broke your positioning down in your Channel HQ dashboard. That's all you need to focus on right now.

Add later

The kids, the hobbies, the cooking, the car rides. Bring them in gradually and experiment as you go. Your audience will tell you what lands.

Skip entirely for now

Rebranding three times before your first upload. Perfect intros. Matching thumbnails. None of it matters at zero videos.

Three ideas to hold onto

Why channels die

Film the story, not just the service

"Retwist on medium locs" competes with everyone. "She hadn't had a retwist in 8 months, here's what we found" is a video only you can make.

Your one sentence

I help ___ do ___ so they can ___.

Example: "I help people with locs understand their hair so they stop guessing and start growing healthy locs." Post yours in the community this week.

How people find you

Search · Browse · Suggested

Search: they typed a question. Browse: YouTube put you on their home page. Suggested: you showed up next to another video. Beginners win on search first.

Try your one sentence

I help ___ ___ so they can ___.

Segment 6 · Let's build it

Set up your channel

Follow along in YouTube Studio. If your channel already exists, use this as your clean-up list.

Demo Share your screen in Studio → Customization. Walk through each field on your own channel live, then give them 10 minutes to do theirs while you answer questions.

  1. Create or open your channel

    Sign in to YouTube with the Google account you'll use for the business → profile picture → Create a channel (or Your channel if it exists). Use a business email, not a personal one you might lose access to.

  2. Verify your phone number

    YouTube Studio → Settings → Channel → Feature eligibility. Verifying unlocks custom thumbnails and videos longer than 15 minutes. Do this tonight.

  3. Channel name

    Studio → Customization → Profile. Use the name people already know you by. Your business name, your name, or both ("Clutch | ClutchNLoc"). Adding your trade or city can help search.

  4. Handle

    Same screen. Make it match your Instagram and TikTok if you can, so people can find you anywhere with one name.

  5. Description

    Up to 1,000 characters. Lead with your one sentence, then who you are, where you work, what you post, and your booking link. Use the template below.

  6. Links

    Customization → Profile → Links. Booking first, then shop or products, then Instagram and TikTok. The first link shows on your channel header.

  7. Contact email

    Add a business email so brands can reach you for partnerships.

  8. Branding

    Customization → Branding: profile picture, banner, and video watermark. Specs below.

Segment 8 · The door is narrowing

Monetization rules

On February 1, 2027 YouTube doubles the watch-time and Shorts-view requirement for new channels applying to earn ad revenue. Channels already in the program keep their status. This cohort runs the months before that change.

Time left under today's rules

Review takes about a month, so aim to apply well before January 31.

LevelRequirements todayFrom Feb 1, 2027What it unlocks
Starting outAny channelSameLinks in descriptions, booking traffic, brand deals, affiliate links. You can make money from day one, just not from YouTube itself.
Fan funding tier500 subscribers · 3 public uploads in last 90 days · 3,000 watch hours in 12 months or 3M Shorts views in 90 daysUnchangedChannel memberships, Super Chat, Super Stickers, Super Thanks, YouTube Shopping for your own products
Full YPP (ad revenue)1,000 subscribers · 4,000 watch hours in 12 months or 10M Shorts views in 90 days1,000 subscribers · 8,000 watch hours in 365 days or 20M Shorts views in 90 daysAd revenue and YouTube Premium revenue on long-form and Shorts
Already in YPP—Status kept. Must accept the updated terms in Studio by Jan 31, 2027Shorts ad revenue will need 10M qualified Shorts views per 90 days to keep earning on Shorts

Shorts views count toward subscribers, but Shorts watch time does not count toward long-form watch hours.

Segment 10 · Getting ahead · Week 2 · Wed, Oct 28

The Blueprint + Back Catalog

You already have videos. They're sitting in your camera roll from Instagram and TikTok. Let's get them on YouTube as Shorts this week.

Your three pillars

Where your trade, your hobbies, and your point of view overlap. Your Channel HQ already maps this. You're only confirming it, not starting from scratch.

  • Pillar 1: your craft
  • Pillar 2: your business or how you work
  • Pillar 3: you (point of view, lifestyle, or a hobby you'll actually keep filming)

Cadence that matches your real capacity

One long-form video a week that you actually post beats three you abandon by December. Block filming days around your book, not the other way around.

The back catalog sprint

  1. Use the original files

    From your camera roll, not downloads from TikTok or IG. No watermarks.

  2. Swap trending audio

    Popular songs can get claimed. Use YouTube's audio library or your own voice.

  3. Write searchable titles

    What would a client type? "How to fix thinning locs at the root" beats "Obsessed 😍".

  4. Keep them up to 3 minutes

    Shorts can run up to 3 minutes, vertical or square.

  5. Link each Short to a long-form video

    Once you have one, use the related video link so Shorts viewers land on your long-form.

  6. Schedule 1–2 a day

    Don't dump 30 at once. Schedule them out so the channel looks active for weeks.

Your camera roll is already a content library

This was an Instagram video. With the original file and a searchable title, it can go up as a Short this week. See how I post mine on my Shorts tab.

See my Shorts ↗
How many videos are sitting in your camera roll right now that nobody on YouTube has seen?

What Shorts count toward

  • Yes: subscribers
  • No: long-form watch hours

Repurposing old client clips

These already went public on IG or TikTok, so you can repost them. Skip anything a client has asked you to take down. Going forward, new clients sign your media consent form.

Channel trailer and featured video

Customization → Layout. Set a channel trailer for people who haven't subscribed (who you are, what you post, why stay) and a featured video for returning subscribers. Your intro voice note from this week's homework is the start of your trailer.

Your 13-week roadmap

Five phases, thirteen weeks. By graduation you'll have a branded, posting channel wired into your business.

  2. Planning + Production

  3. Post-Production

  5. Integration

The questions everyone asks

Real talk

Use my personal channel or start a new one?

If your current channel already has your work on it, keep it and clean it up. If it's mostly unrelated stuff, start fresh with your business email. Either way, set it up so you can add a manager or editor later without sharing your password.

Do I have to show my face?

No. Hands, work, and your voice can carry a tutorial. But your face builds trust fastest. If you're nervous, start with voice and hands and work up to it.

Should I delete my old videos?

Usually no. Watch time on videos you delete or make private stops counting toward monetization. If something is truly off-brand, set it to unlisted instead.

What if clients in my city see it?

That's the point. Local clients finding you is the business win. Your "How did you find me?" question will show you exactly how many.

How often do I have to post?

As often as you can keep up. One long-form a week that you actually post beats three a week that stop in December. Shorts from your back catalog fill the gaps.

Do I need to buy gear first?

No. Start with your phone. Buy gear when you know what's actually slowing you down.

Questions for the room

Go around, or drop answers in the chat.

  1. What made you finally say yes to YouTube?
  2. What's the question you answer in your chair every single week?
  3. What's one piece of misinformation you're tired of correcting?
  4. Who do you want to be known as online in one year?
  5. What's scaring you most about showing up on camera?
  6. Which income stream do you want YouTube to feed first: bookings, classes, products, or partnerships?
  7. What part of your life outside the chair would you be open to sharing someday?
  8. What's one thing you'll have done before co-work on Thursday?
